Another objection is that abolishing marriage would leave vulnerable partners, especially economically dependent ones, unprotected at the end of a relationship. That concern deserves serious attention, but it is not an argument for preserving legal marriage as such. It is an argument for clear default rules governing shared property, cohabitation, caregiving reliance, and economic dependency. Those protections can be drafted directly and applied where the facts justify them. Indeed, doing so may be fairer than current divorce law, which often produces arbitrary results by assuming that all marriages generate the same expectations. A robust system of domestic contracts, cohabitation law, equitable remedies, and dependency protections could protect vulnerable parties without granting marriage a unique legal status.

In fact, abolition would likely expose and reduce many pathologies created by marriage law. Because marriage is surrounded by legal incentives, people often enter it hastily, strategically, or under social and economic pressure. Because it is a sweeping legal status, dissolution becomes expensive, adversarial, and bureaucratic. Because it is publicly recognized and idealized, people may remain in harmful relationships due to fear of legal complexity or stigma. A legal system based on modular agreements and defined obligations would make relationships more transparent. People would know which commitments they had actually made, rather than inheriting a dense package of rules many barely understand when they marry.

There is also a democratic argument for abolition. Marriage law inevitably turns private life into a political battleground. Every election can become a contest over who deserves recognition, what counts as a family, and which moral views the law will endorse. This politicization is corrosive. It tempts majorities to impose their values on minorities and encourages citizens to seek validation through state recognition. But the government should not be the arbiter of personal worth. By withdrawing from marriage altogether, the state would lower the stakes of cultural disagreement and leave space for civil society, faith communities, families, and individuals to organize intimate life according to their own convictions.

Abolition would also better reflect modern diversity. Contemporary life includes single-parent homes, blended families, unmarried couples, queer chosen families, co-parenting arrangements, multigenerational households, intentional communities, and lifelong non-romantic partnerships. The legal centrality of marriage no longer corresponds to social reality, if it ever truly did. Preserving it as the privileged gateway to rights and recognition sends the message that these other relationships are secondary or deficient. A just legal order should not encode a hierarchy of intimacy. It should facilitate voluntary arrangements and protect actual dependency wherever it exists.

Of course, abolishing state marriage would require substantial legal reform. But difficulty is not a refutation. Many outdated institutions persist because lawmakers prefer patchwork fixes to principled redesign. The transition could be managed by replacing marriage-based rules with systems for designated beneficiaries, parental registration, domestic partnership contracts, dependency-based benefits, cohabitation protections, and individualized estate planning defaults. Existing marriages could be converted into civil unions or domestic contracts during a transition period, while religious and personal marriages continue entirely outside state control. What matters is the principle: the state should stop conferring a special legal identity called marriage.

Ultimately, legal marriage is an anachronism. It is a relic of a time when the state sought to structure sexuality, gender roles, inheritance, and family life through a single official institution. Even after many reforms, its logic remains paternalistic. A liberal society should not ask permission to love, commit, cohabit, care, or build a family. The law should govern concrete matters—property, parentage, care, consent, dependency, and obligation—without annexing the deeply personal concept of marriage.

Marriage belongs to individuals, families, cultures, and religious communities, not to the government. Let churches define it. Let communities celebrate it. Let couples cherish it or reject it. But let the state step aside. Abolishing the legal institution of marriage would not demean commitment; it would liberate commitment from bureaucratic control. It would not weaken families; it would force the law to support real caregiving and responsibility rather than symbolic status. And it would not create chaos; it would replace a blunt, exclusionary institution with a more honest and flexible legal framework. For the sake of freedom, fairness, and pluralism, marriage should be removed entirely from the law.

Introduction

On one side, we have the libertarian libertines—the ones who believe marriage is just a social construct, a government-issued certificate of approval for people who still think "I do" means something beyond a tax deduction. On the other side? The marriage defenders—the ones who clutch their pearls (or their wedding rings) and scream, "But marriage is sacred! The state must protect it!"

Let’s talk about the real hypocrisy of the marriage defenders. Because if you’re going to argue that the government should be involved in marriage, you have to accept some pretty absurd consequences—and none of them are pretty.

1. "But Marriage is a Fundamental Right!"

Oh, really? Then why does the state only recognize heterosexual unions? Why does it ignore same-sex couples, polyamorous relationships, or even the fact that many people just don’t want to get married at all? If marriage is a fundamental right, then why does the government have to force people to participate? Why isn’t it just a choice, like whether to wear a tie to a wedding or not?

And let’s be honest—if marriage is so sacred, why does the state tax it? Why does it regulate it? Why does it punish people for not conforming to its definition? If marriage is just a social contract, then why does the government have to intervene to make sure everyone plays by the same rules?

2. "But What About Children?"

Ah, the classic defense. "Marriage is for children!" Well, sure, but so is child support, and the state already enforces that. So why does the government need to certify who is and isn’t a parent? Why can’t a single mom or a polyamorous family just prove they’re raising kids without needing a government stamp of approval?

And let’s not forget—many people choose not to get married because they don’t want the government’s approval. They want to live their lives, have kids, and raise them without the state’s interference. If marriage is so important for children, why doesn’t the state just fund them instead of requiring them?

3. "But What About Divorce?"

Oh, the divorce defense. "But what if the marriage fails?" Well, then the state can just divorce the marriage, right? No big deal. But here’s the thing—if marriage is just a contract, then why does the state have to intervene to dissolve it? Why can’t people just break up like any other relationship without needing a judge’s approval?

And let’s talk about divorce rates. If marriage is so stable, why do so many people get divorced? If the state is so invested in marriage, why does it have to punish people for failing at it? Why doesn’t it just say, "Congratulations, you failed at marriage. Now go find a new one."

4. "But What About Religion?"

Ah, the religious exemption. "But marriage is a religious institution!" Well, sure, but so is taxation, and the state already has to deal with that. If religion is so important, why does the state have to ignore it when it comes to marriage? Why can’t people just marry in their own way without needing a government license?

And let’s be real—most people who get married aren’t religious. They’re just people who want to legally commit to each other. If marriage is so sacred, why does the state have to force people to participate?

5. "But What About the Economy?"

Ah, the economic argument. "But marriage boosts the economy!" Well, sure, but so does taxation, and the state already has to deal with that. If marriage is so important for the economy, why does the state have to regulate it? Why can’t people just marry and live their lives without needing a government stamp of approval?

And let’s not forget—many people choose not to get married because they don’t want the government’s approval. They want to live their lives, have kids, and raise them without the state’s interference. If marriage is so important for the economy, why doesn’t the state just fund it instead of requiring it?

Conclusion: The State Should Just Go Away

So there you have it—the real hypocrisy of the marriage defenders. They want the state to be involved in marriage, but they don’t want the state to be involved in anything else. They want the state to protect marriage, but they don’t want the state to punish people for not conforming to its definition. They want the state to fund marriage, but they don’t want the state to tax it.

If marriage is so important, why does the state have to intervene? Why can’t people just marry and live their lives without needing a government stamp of approval? The answer is simple: The state doesn’t belong in the bedroom.

So next time someone tries to tell you that the state should be involved in marriage, just ask them this: "If marriage is so sacred, why does the state have to force people to participate?" And watch them squirm.

Prompt:
Write a detailed persuasive essay strongly arguing in favor of the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, asserting that marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and treated solely as a private relationship or contract.
Model Response:

Marriage is one of the most legally entrenched institutions in modern societies, yet its status is rarely questioned at the root. We debate who may marry, how many may marry, under what conditions they may divorce—but we almost never confront the more radical and compelling question: Why should the state regulate, define, privilege, or recognize marriage at all?

A persuasive case can be made that it should not. The state’s role in marriage is historically contingent, ethically problematic, administratively distortive, and socially harmful. Marriage should be removed from the legal sphere entirely and treated solely as a private relationship or set of relationships—governed by voluntary contracts, religious or cultural practices where desired, and general laws that apply to all persons regardless of romantic status.

To argue for the complete abolition of state-recognized marriage is not to attack love, commitment, family, or mutual care. It is, in fact, to respect them more deeply—by freeing them from political gatekeeping, arbitrary legal privilege, and a model that no longer matches the diversity of real human lives.

  1. Historical contingency and moral overreach

The modern assumption that marriage is a civil status granted, regulated, and tracked by the state is relatively recent and culturally parochial. For much of human history, intimate partnerships were handled by families, religious institutions, or community norms, not centralized bureaucracies. The strong legal fusion of “marriage” and “state” emerges sharply with:

  • The rise of centralized states seeking to manage inheritance, property, and legitimacy of offspring.
  • Religious-political alliances turning marriage into a tool of moral enforcement.
  • Racial and eugenic controls (e.g., bans on interracial marriage, compulsory marriage norms).
  • Gendered control of women’s bodies, sexuality, and economic dependency.

The state did not step into marriage to celebrate love; it stepped in to control people and resources. That history matters. When the state confers a special civil status called “marriage,” it:

  • Takes a particular vision of intimate life (dyadic, sexual, lifelong, domestic, normatively reproductive).
  • Elevates that vision above others through legal privileges and recognition.
  • Imposes gatekeeping power: who counts, who is excluded, and which bonds are seen as legitimate.

Even when reformed (for example, expanding marriage to same-sex couples), the underlying principle remains: the state presumes authority to define and distribute legitimacy in the most intimate domain of human existence. That is a profound overreach.

If individuals are legal adults, capable of forming contracts, raising children, owning property, and associating freely, then the idea that they must secure state permission for the “correct” structure of their intimate commitments is philosophically indefensible. The state has legitimate interests in preventing harm, enforcing contracts, and protecting dependents; it does not have a legitimate interest in deciding which consensual relationships are worthy of special status.

  1. Marriage as legal privilege and structural discrimination

State-recognized marriage is not a neutral mechanism. It is a vast complex of privileges and default rules that systematically advantages some citizens over others based solely on their intimate choices.

Marriage status determines or affects:

  • Tax treatment
  • Immigration and residency rights
  • Inheritance rights and intestacy defaults
  • Hospital visitation and medical decision-making
  • Social security, pensions, health insurance, and employment benefits
  • Parental presumptions and custody defaults
  • Liability protections and testimonial privileges

These benefits are not awarded because married people necessarily contribute more to society, love more deeply, or care more effectively. They are awarded because they participate in a state-sanctioned relational form. The result is:

  • Privileging romantic/sexual dyads over friendships, extended kinship networks, non-romantic life partners, multi-adult households, and chosen families.
  • Penalizing people who, for moral, religious, political, or personal reasons, do not wish to marry.
  • Reinforcing a hierarchy of relationships in which “married couple” is at the pinnacle and other forms of care and interdependence are formally devalued.

This is structural discrimination. It says to citizens: organize your intimate life in this specific configuration, or accept second-class access to rights and protections. When benefits, protections, and legal conveniences are tied to marital status, they are not being distributed on a just basis (such as need, dependence, contribution, or vulnerability) but on conformity to a state-blessed model of life.

The solution is not endlessly expanding who may marry in order to chase inclusivity within an inherently exclusionary framework. The principled solution is to abolish state marriage as a special legal category, and design laws that protect people based on their actual relationships, agreements, and dependencies—without requiring them to pass through a symbolic ritual of state approval.

  1. Autonomy, pluralism, and freedom of association

A liberal, pluralistic society should respect diverse conceptions of the good life. Yet state-recognized marriage exerts soft coercion: it channels people into one state-defined template as the preferred route to legal security, social respectability, and economic advantages.

This undermines:

  • Individual autonomy: Adults should design their own commitments—romantic, platonic, sexual, communal—without legal penalty for nonconformity.
  • Cultural and religious pluralism: Different communities have different ideas of marriage’s meaning. A unitary state form suppresses this diversity or creates perpetual conflict over whose definition wins.
  • Freedom of association: The law should facilitate voluntary associations and contracts, not anoint one archetype as uniquely valid.

By removing marriage from state control, we:

  • Allow religious organizations to define marriage according to their doctrines, without forcing nonadherents to live under those norms.
  • Allow secular individuals and communities to create their own partnership agreements, rituals, and values.
  • Protect those who reject marriage altogether from informal coercion baked into law and policy.

Critically, this is not an argument for deregulated chaos. It is an argument for neutral regulation: the state upholds contracts, enforces obligations, and protects vulnerable parties—without prescribing a privileged pattern for intimate life.

  1. Protecting dependents without marital status

A common objection is that state recognition of marriage is necessary to protect vulnerable spouses and children: to ensure support, clarify parentage, and handle property. This is both empirically and conceptually mistaken, and it exposes an important point: the state’s legitimate interests can be served better without marital status.

We already possess, or can easily construct, neutral mechanisms that do not require “marriage” as a special status:

  • Parentage laws:

    • Parent-child relationships deserve robust legal recognition and obligations regardless of whether parents are married.
    • Laws can define parentage based on biology, intent to parent, adoption, and established caregiving relationships.
    • There is no rational reason that a romantic/marital relationship between adults should condition a child’s rights.

  • Support and property:

    • Cohabitation, shared assets, and economic interdependence can be governed by contract, default partnership statutes, and unjust enrichment doctrines.
    • Adults who share life and resources can opt into standardized civil partnership contracts (not “marriage” but generic cohabitation/partnership agreements open to friends, relatives, or multiple parties).
    • Upon dissolution, courts can apply clear, content-neutral rules about division of property and support based on contribution, agreements, and reliance—without mystifying it as “divorce.”

  • Care, decision-making, and next-of-kin:

    • Every adult should have the right to designate, by simple default forms, who can:
      • Visit them in hospitals
      • Make medical decisions if they are incapacitated
      • Act as their emergency contact
      • Manage their affairs
    • These rights should not hinge on marital status but on explicit designation—something a fair legal system should encourage for all.

Abolishing state marriage does not abandon vulnerable spouses; it forces the law to protect vulnerability directly, rather than using marriage as a crude proxy. Instead of “Are you married?” the law must ask: “What commitments have you made? Who depends on whom? What agreements and expectations were reasonably formed?”

This approach improves justice: it no longer neglects those who are functionally spouses but legally unmarried, nor does it grant protections automatically to a spouse who, in practice, contributed nothing and assumed no real burden of care.

  1. Ending the moralization and politicization of intimacy

Because the state controls marriage, marriage becomes a perpetual battleground for cultural warfare:

  • Fights over same-sex marriage, interracial marriage, trans-inclusive marriage, age gaps, and non-monogamous structures are intensified because “marriage” is not just a private or religious status; it is a state-backed symbol of legitimacy.
  • Every expansion of marriage becomes a victory; every exclusion becomes a state-enforced stigma.

If the state withdrew from marriage:

  • Religious communities could maintain their own definitions: some recognizing only heterosexual unions, others embracing same-sex or plural unions, others rejecting the institution entirely.
  • Secular people could create commitments without clerical or governmental approval.
  • Political fights over “who gets to marry” would largely evaporate because the state would no longer be in the business of blessing relationships.

Crucially, this reduces the power of any majority—religious, secular, conservative, progressive—to weaponize the machinery of the state to impose its moral or metaphysical view of marriage on everyone.

  1. Better fit for contemporary relationships

The world that state marriage was built for—a male breadwinner, a female homemaker, lifelong monogamy, clear gender roles—is gone or going. Today we have:

  • Dual-earner couples with complex property arrangements.
  • Cohabiting partners who function as families without marrying.
  • Single parents and blended families.
  • Chosen families that share care among friends or community members.
  • Polyamorous households and multi-adult caregiving groups.
  • People who value commitment but reject the symbolic baggage of “marriage.”

Yet the law continues to elevate one model: a two-person, romantically and sexually exclusive partnership, solemnized by a licensed authority. Everyone else’s reality is forced into this mold, ignored, or precariously patched with ad hoc workarounds.

Abolishing state marriage allows the legal system to align with actual human practice:

  • Offer modular legal tools: cohabitation agreements, caregiving compacts, shared-property regimes, parental intention declarations, medical proxy forms.
  • Allow any set of consenting adults—not only romantic couples—to choose from these tools and configure them to match their real relationships.
  • Respect that not all deep commitments are sexual, and not all sexual relationships are or should be deep legal commitments.

Rather than stretching “marriage” until it loses all coherence, we can discard it as a legal category and replace it with precise, inclusive, contract-based mechanisms.

  1. Answering the key objections

Objection 1: Marriage is foundational to social stability; abolishing it would cause chaos.

Response:

  • Social stability is produced by functioning relationships, reliable caregiving, economic security, and clear legal frameworks—not by a specific word printed on a certificate.
  • The proposal is not to abolish commitment or contracts, but to decouple them from a privileged, morally loaded status.
  • Countries already cope with large proportions of non-marital cohabitation and children born outside marriage; administrative solutions exist and work.
  • A transition could be orderly:
    • Convert existing marriages into default partnership contracts.
    • Maintain all underlying obligations while phasing out marriage as a special category.
    • Communicate clearly that love, family, and mutual care remain fully protected.

Objection 2: Children need married parents; abolishing marriage undermines the family.

Response:

  • What children need is stable, loving, responsible caregivers and legal recognition of those caregivers.
  • Research overwhelmingly emphasizes parenting quality, economic security, and absence of abuse—not the mere marital status of adults.
  • By recognizing parental obligations directly, independently of marital status, we strengthen child protection.
  • Tying child well-being to whether adults performed a legal-ritualistic act is irrational and punishes children for adults’ choices.

Objection 3: But people want marriage; why take it away?

Response:

  • No one is proposing to abolish marriage as a personal, cultural, or religious practice.
  • Couples (or groups) could still call themselves married, celebrate weddings, and belong to traditions that treat those unions as sacred.
  • What is being abolished is the state’s special recognition and package of privileges—not the human phenomenon of committing one’s life to another.
  • Removing state recognition levels the field: your marriage’s meaning comes from your values and community, not governmental endorsement.

Objection 4: Without marriage, people might not commit, harming social cohesion.

Response:

  • Commitment grounded in authentic choice, not tax policy or visa status, is more robust.
  • If a relationship only persists because of legal perks or exit penalties, that is not a moral success story—it is coerced stability.
  • A system of clear, opt-in contracts lets people signal commitment transparently while preserving the freedom to decline obligations they do not endorse.
  1. Towards a post-marriage legal order

What does a coherent alternative look like?

Key elements:

  • Neutral personal status:
    • No “married” or “single” in law—only “adult persons” with particular contracts, dependents, and designations.
  • Contract-based partnerships:
    • Simple, accessible legal instruments for:
      • Shared property regimes
      • Mutual support obligations
      • Inheritance arrangements
      • Co-residency and financial pooling
    • Open to any consenting adults, not restricted to sexual/romantic pairings or fixed to the number two.
  • Robust family and child law:
    • Parentage determined by biology, adoption, or intentional caregiving arrangements.
    • Automatic child support obligations for parents, irrespective of any relationship between them.
    • Secure recognition for multi-parent families where multiple adults intentionally take on parental roles.
  • Designated decision-makers:
    • Default rules that prioritize designated persons for medical decisions, visitation, and next-of-kin roles, chosen directly by each adult.
  • Social benefits disentangled from marital status:
    • Health insurance, immigration sponsorship, tax relief, and pensions based on:
      • Individual circumstances (income, disability, age).
      • Caregiving responsibilities (children, disabled relatives, elders).
      • Explicit sponsorship or dependency contracts.
    • This ensures support goes where it is morally relevant—need and care—not where it is romantically traditional.

Such a framework is fairer, more transparent, less intrusive, and more adaptable to real human lives than a one-size-fits-all institution administered by the state.

Conclusion: Love doesn’t need a license; justice doesn’t need a wedding ring.

The continued existence of state-recognized marriage rests on inertia, sentimentality, and historical habit more than on principled justification. When scrutinized, it is:

  • An instrument of moralizing control over intimate life.
  • A source of unjust legal privilege and structural discrimination.
  • An inadequate and outdated proxy for the things the law should really care about: consent, obligation, dependency, care, and harm.

By abolishing marriage as a legal institution and treating intimate bonds as private relationships and/or explicit contracts, we would:

  • Affirm individual autonomy and pluralism.
  • End state favoritism for one particular form of life.
  • Protect children and vulnerable persons more directly and effectively.
  • Defuse culture wars waged over who gets access to a politically consecrated status.
  • Align the law with the actual diversity of human relationships.

Love, commitment, and family are too important to be policed by the state. Let the law mind justice—contracts, rights, obligations, protection from harm—and let marriage, in all its varied meanings, belong to the people, their communities, and their consciences alone.

The practical justifications for state marriage crumble under scrutiny. Proponents cite three main pillars: the welfare of children, economic protections, and social cohesion. Each is a phantom justification.

First, children’s welfare. The well-being of a child depends on the quality of parenting, not the marital status of the parents. Second, economic and legal efficiencies. Couples rely on marriage for automatic inheritance rights, spousal privilege in court, hospital visitation, and tax benefits. We can write laws that allow individuals to designate any person as their default heir, medical proxy, or beneficiary through a simple, revocable legal form.
